newsitem.title: USA: IBM sets aggressive plan for cash mountain.
newsitem.headline: IBM sets aggressive plan for cash mountain.

text.p: Fresh on the heels of its blockbuster first quarter, International Business Machines Corp on Tuesday laid out a plan to return much of its $6.4 billion mountain of cash to shareholders.

The announcements, which include a $3.5 billion addition to Big Blue's stock buyback budget and a 14 percent dividend increase, helped settle questions over what IBM would do with its cash and could help the blue chip tech giant retain the momentum it recently recaptured on Wall Street.
"They're clearly signalling they want to stay more aggressive with the share repurchase program," said John Jones, an analyst at Salomon Brothers. "That should help earnings per share a lot."

The effects of previous buybacks were evident in IBM's recently reported first quarter, which showed earnings per share rising to $2.37 from $2.21 even as net income slipped to $1.20 billion from $1.21 billion.
The difference was a sharp fall in shares outstanding, due in large part to $2 billion in first quarter share buybacks.

The new buybacks met with general enthusiasm, if not surprise, as analysts noted the effort extends an ongoing policy at Big Blue. Importantly, they said, IBM's acts were those of a company assured in its outlook.

"This is obviously a vote of confidence by management in the prospects for this company," said William Milton, an analyst at Brown Brothers Harriman. "If the company were not confident of its prospects, it wouldn't be making this kind of commitment."
That IBM opted to raise its dividend was perhaps the more surprising, and symbolic, of the two moves.
The increase -- which brings the payout to $1.60 per share per year from $1.40 -- brings the annual dividend yield to about one percent based on current trading levels.
That is less than most of the 30 Dow industrials but more than many shares in the growth-oriented tech sector.
"It's still a low yield, but that's typical for technology companies," said Wendy Abramowitz, an analyst at Argus Research.
Indeed, some analysts expressed puzzlement over the dividend increase, which they viewed as cosmetic at best.

"The dividend isn't all that much money," said Gary Helmig, an analyst at SoundView Financial. "$25 million per quarter is hardly measurable for them, which makes you wonder why they're doing it at all."

Shareholders appeared pleased with the developments. IBM shares jumped 5-1/4 to 155-5/8 in early afternoon of a session that saw the Dow surge more than 100 points. About half IBM's rally came in the moments immediately after news of its plans.
